title: My experience in the Yamate Japanese Exchange Program: A journey of culture, connection and change | Columnists | yakimaherald.com
text:
This summer, I had the incredible opportunity to travel to Japan as part of the Yamate Japanese Exchange Program between the Yakima School District and Yamate Gakuin of Yokohama, Japan.
From July 18 to Aug. 2, I joined 30 students from Davis, Eisenhower and East Valley high schools for a two-week whirlwind of culture shock, spiritual enlightenment and vending machine addiction. We explored everything from neon-lit cities like Tokyo and Yokohama, to historic enclaves like Kamakura and Enoshima.
And, let me tell you, those 14 days felt like a mini lifetime.
I won’t pretend I walked into Japan as a fluent speaker. Unless you count pointing, bowing, or dramatic charades as fluent communication, I was mostly flying blind. Luckily, my host family – a kind mom, dad, and their 16-year-old son, Naoaki – didn’t mind my linguistic flailing.
My roommate, Eisenhower student Brandon Etherage, and I found connection in the little things: late-night convenience store runs, shared inside jokes, and a collective struggle to decode train maps that looked like rainbow spaghetti.
Brandon also performed in Yamate's 50th-year band competition as a trumpet player, adding a special touch of musical diplomacy to our exchange.
Shopping
Shopping during the Japan trip became a borderline sport. One of my favorite haunts was the Shonan Terrace Mall in Tsujido. While others were picking out cute stationery and keychains, I bought 11 Rubik’s Cubes. Yes, 11. Including a limited-edition 50th anniversary Japan-exclusive cube. You could say I found my true calling in speedcubing under a blanket-covered kotatsu table.
My suitcase came home less like luggage and more like a portable puzzle museum.
Speaking of packing: I started this trip like an amateur optimist. I had 14 outfits in a suitcase with half the space left open, thinking I’d “pack light and buy what I need.” Cut to the return flight: me, desperately Tetris-ing souvenirs, snacks and mystery anime merch into a 35-pound bag, while sneakily stuffing heavy items into my carry-on like a smuggler evading TSA.
I now have mad respect for origami artists and professional movers.
The sights of Japan
But the trip wasn’t all shopping and suitcase strategy. We ventured out on four major excursions that blended education, entertainment and unexpected cardio. At Hakone National Park, we marveled at misty views of Mount Fuji, which occasionally played peekaboo behind the clouds.
Cultural Day at Yamate Gakuin High School introduced us to Shakyo (also known as the practice of hand-copying Buddhist sutras), traditional matcha tea ceremonies, the random fortunes known as omikuji that are written on strips of paper, and dressing in a kimono.
Imagine trying to wrap yourself in 10 layers of kimono elegance while praying you don’t trip. It was a graceful exercise in controlled panic and cultural appreciation.
Another highlight was our group trip to Asakusa in Tokyo. This is a historic, bustling marketplace filled with temples, tourist traps and heavenly street food.
We were also supposed to take a river cruise, but Tokyo traffic had other plans. Apparently, gridlock is Japan’s version of a plot twist.
Our final excursion was to DisneySea, which, despite us arriving late (again: traffic!), delivered a magical evening filled with exactly two rides, some sugary snacks, and more selfies than I’m proud of.
Sheltering under a tsunami warning
On July 30, a tsunami warning was issued after a magnitude 8.8 megathrust earthquake struck near the Kamchatka Peninsula. Although it didn’t hit Japan directly, the country’s meticulous emergency systems kicked in. We were escorted to Kamakura City Hall, where we sheltered for four hours before walking 90 minutes home in the blazing sun.
Picture a slow, sweaty parade of Americans rethinking their shoe choices.
But, as intense as it was, it brought our group closer together. Nothing says “bonding” like natural disasters and vending machine lunches.
Japan weather
Speaking of weather: The heat and humidity were no joke. Even 85°F felt like 105°F when paired with 90% humidity. You haven’t truly lived until you’ve sweated through your clothes just standing still.
Luckily, Japan’s vending machine game is top-tier. They’re ubiquitous. Like, one every 50 feet. Water, tea, juice, the Pocari Sweat sports drink -- all cold, and all under a dollar. Lifesavers. Literal lifesavers.
Experiencing new food
Food was a cultural adventure of its own. From unagi sushi and tonkatsu ramen to takoyaki (a surprisingly tasty minced octopus snack shaped into small balls), every meal was a new experience. Dining out was cheap, delicious and omnipresent. I might have eaten 200% more rice in two weeks than I have in my entire life.
And chopsticks? I went from fumbling like Edward Scissorhands to becoming a precision-level noodle ninja.
By the end, I was confidently slurping udon noodles and slicing mochi rice cakes with surgical dexterity.
Transportation differences
Transportation was another eye-opener. Most people walk, bike or take the train, and traffic somehow functions with roads that look like narrow driveways.
The trains were shockingly efficient, even when they were filled beyond what seemed like human capacity. I’m pretty sure some mornings I was held up by air pressure alone. The sheer synchronicity of the transit system felt like clockwork choreography on a national scale.
Yamate Gakuin High School
We also got to experience daily life at Yamate Gakuin High School. We observed classes, attended cultural sessions, and spent time with students who were just as curious about our lives as we were about theirs.
From classroom etiquette to club activities, it was fascinating to witness the fusion of tradition and modernity in Japanese education. Everyone we met – students, families, staff – welcomed us with open arms, humble hearts and lots of snacks.
The best part? It never felt like we were just visitors. We were included. Appreciated. Embraced. Whether it was learning to write our names in kanji characters, bonding with our host siblings over music, or simply sitting around the dinner table laughing at mispronunciations, it all felt real and meaningful.
The experience's impact
This exchange taught me far more than I expected. I gained confidence, global awareness, lifelong friendships, and a new understanding of what it means to be a respectful guest in another country.
Going to Japan showed me how much we can learn when we step outside our comfort zones, and how rewarding it is to embrace the unfamiliar with open eyes and an open heart.
Massive thanks to Yakima School District director of communications Kirsten Fitterer and to Davis High School Assistant Principal Lorenzo Alvarado for organizing this amazing program and making it accessible to students like me.
If I could, I’d do it all over again. Same suitcase. Same city. Same sense of wonder.
OK, maybe fewer Rubik’s Cubes.
But no promises.
• Theron Clements is an incoming junior at Davis High School.
